utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning to you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the staff of the Registry, the members of the Prosecution and the Defence counsel; good morning to the accused. This morning we start off with the Defence case of the accused Mr. Zigic. I am now going to give the floor, without further ado, to Mr. Stojanovic for an opening statement, I think, according to Rule 84. Is that right, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, and thank you for giving me the floor. If I may reserve the right to address other issues with respect to the decisions that we have received in the meantime, but as you have so rightly stated, Your Honour, first things first, and it is my opening statement that is first now. Your Honours, it is no easy task to make the right selection of what the Defence of Mr. Zoran Zigic should say precisely at this particular moment. One must be all-embracing, but procedure is something that in itself implies dynamics so that everything has a proper time, and we are going to bear that in mind now. Basically, in summary fashion, we wish to indicate some of our viewpoints with respect to what is contained in the indictment, to what has been done so far, as well as to the intentions and goals which we wish to achieve through, to use the terminology of common law procedure, our own case. A portion of our principal views the Defence of Zoran Zigic has already demonstrated in its motion for judgement of acquittal, which will mutatis mutandis further be very topical in our line of defence. There are two bases upon which our Defence case rests. First, an active quest for the truth in the events that took place; and second, a careful legal analysis of ascertained facts and the logical links between them. Let us say quite frankly at the outset the truth will sometimes be painful for our client, but we are deeply convinced only in a disproportionately small fraction of what he is charged with in the indictment. However, the truth is something that Mr. Zigic personally does not wish to get away from and that is where lies his motive, that after an insight into the two indictments by which he is charged, he himself requested to be transferred to The Hague and to be tried before this Tribunal. According to psychological expertise conducted on the part of two experts which were appointed by the Registry, Mr. Zigic is an exceptionally intelligent individual. Therefore, he must certainly have known that what he has been charged with in two indictments is sufficient to bring the most severe punishment to him. Why, then, did he request to be transferred to The Hague and to be tried according to those indictments? The answer is a simple one. He knew that he did very few of all those things that he's been charged with, and believing that in view of the scope and seriousness of the procedure which is conducted before this Tribunal, the truth will out. We cannot say in this respect that he had any illusions as to his responsibility, which sometimes appears here with individuals who are not the direct perpetrators of acts and who are individuals of a higher rank. Quite simply, he knows very well himself whether he beat somebody up, tortured anybody, or killed anybody, and it is in keeping with those experiences of his that he has asked precisely to be transferred to The Hague. Within the scope of all this, he had the honour of having the distinguished President of this Trial Chamber realise this transfer by a decision of his. A legal analysis and the application of logical principles represent the terrain where the Defence will wage a great battle with the charges of the indictment. It is easy to find answers in the conflict between right and wrong, justice and injustice, although there too quantitative assessments are frequently the subject of great divergence of opinion, but it is far more difficult to resolve the conflict of more acceptable legal principles. In the decisions of this Trial Chamber, logics, which can be both legal and the logic which refers to facts alone, without doubt achieves a very high level. The majority would say that it is easy to resolve the conflict between logical and illogical; however, it is precisely there that the greatest dangers lie, luckily, as a rule, more rarely. In a way, non-logic has in its background a logics of its own. In our opinion, this testifies -- this is borne out by the fact that we have conceived the concept and standard of beyond reasonable doubt, and this can be a very relative notion and concept and, in fact, need not guarantee the truth but need only represent the rules of the game, especially so as that standard here is very frequently unjustifiably accepted and is in great correlation with the rule of the balance of probabilities, and all this in the absence of firm traces of the acts committed. We consider that that is most often not sufficient to bring in a decision on somebody's fate and destiny on the basis of that. However, the basic problem is the conflict between the logical and illogical. Much can be explained in many different, acceptable ways. I think that this is something that the distinguished Supreme Court US Judge Holmes noted a long time ago. Yes, we do accept, but we must go further than that, and in that case we must firmly pose the criteria which will give us our priorities. At all events, logics must be linked up, both to the natural sciences and to the social sciences, and be based on the anthropological factor, which gives measure to all things. In itself, however, logics, of course, is not enough. Justice can sometimes be illogical, from the aspects of basic logical principles. It is the position of the Defence that the indictment, to a great extent, is founded on a simplified logic, and logics which leads, in the best of cases, to the possible and probable. However, for conviction, it is, of course, necessary to have something more certain and better thought out. Here and now we are going to indicate, by way of an example, the placement of the so-called common-purpose theory. The Defence at this point has a common goal, of course, with the Prosecution, and that common goal is truth and justice, which is the object to which the Trial Chamber certainly aspires. But truly it has nothing in common with the theory of the Prosecution, with the Prosecution's theory on a common purpose. Essen lynching is far from what the Prosecution is today placing under the theory which was applied in that case. Unfortunately, this theory is put forward in a far more negative sense, that is to say, as something more regressive, an important step back, even if compared to 1945. At that time, the common purpose was viewed in relation to a very concrete event. An immediate and very concrete purpose was sought and not some imaginary one or ideological one. Therefore - and perhaps I'm going to be a little bold in this comparison - the Nazis were in a better position than our client finds himself with respect to this position on the part of the Prosecution and the theory -- the common-purpose theory. Not all Nazis, although there is enough scope for that in the Nuremberg Statute - and especially not the majority of Germans - came under the impact and acts of this theory, although they did have a common purpose, and that common purpose was to conquer the world and to enslave and exterminate many nations. That, as an easier form, implies persecution. At all events, this concept of the theory of a common purpose and criminal liability and possibility has no fulcrum in the Tribunal Statute or common purposes in every -- there are many common purposes in each and every human endeavour, and so in addition to truth and justice, we can, for example, with certainty say -- with a degree of certainty say that a common purpose is the representative of both the Prosecution and the Defence, even, to take it to the furthest point in a legal way, to take money away from the United Nations, to stretch a point. And this would not be untrue. On the contrary, for many people, this is their primary goal, which ensures their family's existence. If, for example, the Defence, along this road towards a common purpose with the Prosecution, towards truth and justice, performs in excess of some kind, then this would mean that the Prosecution would be responsible for that as well. However, this is just an illustration of how we can, in a multitude of ways, nice and not so nice, truthfully show up a large number of common purposes. Common purposes of this kind have a multitude of meanings, and they are relative in the sense of general and particular, for which a theory of -- a common-purpose theory understood in this way has never -- nowhere been accepted in contemporary criminal law. Apart from that, the participation of a number of individuals in a joint transaction is usually everywhere solved by the application of different theories on collaboration. The theory of a common purpose, especially in the sense it is put forward by the other side, quite evidently represents only a massed road to collective responsibility in the sense of responsibility without actually being guilty, and this collective responsibility which in this way can be ascribed to a whole nation. A step further from the individualisation of guilt towards collective responsibility is a step back towards the Middle Ages. On the other hand, it is obvious that it can only have a negative effect on the aims of punishment and judgement. This theory, which frequently does not differentiate between the guilty and the non-guilty, leads to tragedies in criminal law. At all events, it lends a de-stimulative effect on those who refrain from concrete crimes which occur in their environment and those for which there is no adequate mens rea. Generally speaking and independently of the common-purpose theory, the Defence considers that today we cannot rely on the practice of military courts immediately after the end of the Second World War. We are not now living in 1945 or in 1946, and the events are not comparable either. We are prone to sometimes completely agree with the picturesque comparisons one of our colleagues made when he said that the contribution of military courts to the development of law is equal to the contribution of military music to the development of music in general. This Tribunal and these times are at a higher level of society's development and the development of law. Your Honours, the Defence must state that the indictment is not completely clear, especially with respect to what is contained in the confidential and the now-public schedules and attachments to the indictment, as well as the inter-relationship between those documents. On the other hand, apart from one exception and one case, there is a great time span during which the crimes have been allegedly performed, and the Defence, by means of this indictment, has been -- has not been able to practice the defence by alibi. There are no material traces. The documents, documents which sometimes speak importantly about the acts that Zigic is being charged with, similarly do not exist. All that remains for the Defence to do is to put up a defence on the basis of so-called hostile witnesses who, in fact, belong to the indictment or by the testimony of Serbian guards who are themselves the accused or could be accused, but none of these persons does not, in fact, wish to testify, particularly not to say something good about Zigic or to give testimony which would lead to their own culpability, incriminate themselves. All this testifies to the fact that the Defence is in a very adverse position and does not have fair conditions, enjoys fair conditions in a situation which is objectively that way, where we are faced with nobody's guilt. But this gives the Defence the right to request that the Prosecution be placed under the same conditions with somewhat different, otherwise generally accepted, mechanisms. One of those mechanisms is certainly the general assumption in practice throughout the world that somebody cannot be found guilty for the most grievous crimes on the basis of a mere tale told by one or two hostile -- hostilely-disposed witnesses. Now, how does the Defence assess the state of the Prosecution with respect to the Zigic case at this point in time? The Prosecution case has been completed, as well as the cases of the first, second, and third accused. Many hundreds of documents have been admitted into evidence as exhibits and none of them speak of the guilt of the accused Zigic. Several hundred -- several tens of affidavits or written statements have been accepted, of which none speak of any guilt on the part of the accused Zigic. We have heard, I think, 96 witnesses, of whom at least two or three, and then in a contradictory and unacceptable manner, speak about -- testify to some of the counts in the indictment against Zigic. The Defence considers that at this point in time, not a single count of the indictment against Zoran Zigic has been proved by the standard applied of beyond reasonable doubt. How, then, will the Defence of Zigic respond to this? The largest portions in the indictment, the Defence will raise a defence. Serious indictments for serious crimes require a serious defence and serious caution. The Defence cannot rely on the assumption that the Trial Chamber will share its opinion that the standard of beyond reasonable doubt has not been reached, and therefore, with respect to the bulk of the indictment, it will be presenting evidence which dispels doubts and dilemmas as to the existence of acts for which the accused Zigic is being charged. With respect to a smaller portion of the indictment, the Defence will not be putting up a defence, but for that there are two completely opposing reasons. A small section of the indictment the Defence will not be putting up a defence against, although it considers that there is not sufficient proof as to guilt, but it will do so precisely because it considers that those charges and assertions in the indictment are true, and this will be confirmed by Defence witnesses themselves. A second smaller portion of the indictment will similarly not be defended by the Defence because in those sections there is not a trace of truth, and at the same time, not a trace of it in the evidence that has been presented so far. As the case stands at the end of the Prosecution case, and after the presentation of the Defence cases of the three co-accused and how things stand now, we shall illustrate by using one example. We have heard here hundreds of times people mention the three fingers as some form of Serbian greeting. Do we know what those three fingers mean? What does the Honourable Trial Chamber have on that subject in their documents? What does the Honourable Trial Chamber know about that in the almost 10.000 pages of the transcript and many more pages of the different documents? All it has is one single explanation, and that is that given by the testimony of Witness Okis Jasmir given on the 5th of June, 2000 - the page of the transcript is 2549 - that that means one president, one state, and one people. As one would say in German, "ein fuhrer, ein reich, ein volk." Of course, only in Hitler's Germany, where that gesture precisely -- that slogan represented the slogan of Naziism. However, the three fingers, the three fingers salute, represent the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and because of that the people of the Orthodox faith cross themselves with their three fingers. Your Honours, I am not a very religious man, especially not in the classical sense. I say to myself what the great church reformer Martin Luther said, that a good lawyer is a poor Christian probably because many lawyers and men of the law even seek proof for the existence of God. They want to see proof, evidence, documents, stamps, and seals. However, I really found it painful when I heard that a Christian greeting was being turned into something quite different, a Nazi greeting, and that Christianity was being turned into Naziism. At the same time, as a legal man, I found it painful to hear that a basis of this kind should -- a fact of this kind should be presented to the Trial Chamber in this way for them to be able to reach their judgement on that basis. Your Honours, in your documents you have had nothing else, no other explanation for that to the present day, and who knows what else has not been served up to this Trial Chamber by Prosecution witnesses. The Defence will go into greater detail about this in its closing arguments and documents. It has just presented here one example, indicating that, with respect to the Prosecution case, there are exceptional and extraordinary reasons for disbelief and for a maximum degree of caution to be exerted. Without any great desire, and with even less passion, we shall show some of the aspects which will go into some of the aspects of the political and historical context which was the backdrop to this event. There is a multitude of reasons for this premise and point of departure. The reasons for some of this lies in the fact that the previous Defence cases supplied important explanations. A lot has also been ascertained through indisputed fact. However, the basic reason for this starting point is our conviction that the time has come for us to stop trying the politics of the vanquished with the aim of proving that their political options were wrong. This kind of approach to trying criminals of war is very often a requiem of past times. A good or bad political option must never be, and cannot be, justified for torture -- a justification for torture and killing, and it is time for us to begin trying war crimes and to begin trying both political and military victors as well. Nonetheless, in this particular case there is an act which, to a significant measure, is permeated with that which is political, and with historical elements as well, and that is the act from Article 5(H) of our Statute, persecutions on a political, racial, or religious basis. Finally, a very important reason that I do not like to speak about this topic is that it is a highly sensitive one. This Tribunal knows and recognises the measures which can protect those speaking before it from others. However, there are no measures by which to protect others from those who have been given the floor here. By saying that, what I wish to say is that my brief statement on the political and historical context must not be taken to mean a challenge to national chauvinistic passions. It is my true desire that all three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and each and every citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, should live in peace and happiness. That is why my presentations showing the dark side of those relationships represent pure factography, with the aim of giving the Trial Chamber as many facts as possible for it to be able to use those facts for a legal assessment and to be able to do so in a comprehensive manner, with all the facts at hand. The Prosecution has given a partial view of that, in keeping with its own positions in the trial. I think that that is what the Defence should do too. After many decades of peaceful rule on the part of the so-called socialist regime, and the downfall of that option in the Eastern Bloc, we have seen the organisation and victory of nationalistically oriented political parties. It is necessary for me to mention at this point that in the former SFRY, there were approximately 45 per cent Serbs, and in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, prior to the outbreak of the war in 1992, the Serb population made up about one-third. However, the Serbs there had a small part, negligible part. For more than 45 years of the existence of the former SFRY, with the exception of a one-year period, no Serb, not a single Serb, was the president of the country, the country's prime minister, or the number-one man of the Communist Party. A similar picture can be drawn, although not from the very beginning of the existence of the SFRY but from the death of Djuro Pucar, that is to say, 30 years prior to the war it existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina too, this same picture. Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the then Yugoslavia was ruled by numerous Muslims, even more numerous Croats and Slovenes. Josip Broz was, of course, a Croat. Edvard Kardelj was a Slovene. Of the Muslims, let me mention the Dizdarevic brothers, the Pozderac brothers, the Bujedic family. And of the Bosnian Croats, let us mention the Mikulic. All of these were presidents and prime ministers, both with federal and republican power and authority. Of the more important Serbs, we can only mention one, Aleksandar Rankovic, and him up to the 1960s, but he was neither president of the state, nor was he prime minister. But in spite of all this, the Serbs liked the country they had, and they considered themselves to be Yugoslavs. Serb statehood did not exist at all, nor did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any of the Serbs need it. I have to say that it is my personal opinion that the Muslims, too, to the same extent, had this kind of relationship towards that state, the state of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, as has been said, it was then that the extreme nationalistically-oriented parties took centre stage. It is a notorious fact that one nationalism breeds another, that nationalism breeds nationalism, and that is quite logical. In this regard, the Prosecution has consistently been avoiding presenting this Trial Chamber with the order in which these nationalistic parties were established, the parties which quite obviously had almost complete control over their peoples. That is one of the most important facts in all respects. Therefore, Your Honours, let us state this loud and clear here and now: As far as Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, one of the nationalistic parties to be formed was the nationalistic party of the Croats, the HDZ. This was followed by the nationalistic party of the Muslims, the SDA; and finally and lastly, as the last one to be formed, was the nationalistic party of the Serbs, the SDS. I would say in response to the nationalist tensions that had been integrated by the establishment of the two previous nationalist parties. The Prosecution has provided us with abundant information about wartime propaganda. Of course, only about the Serb propaganda, but not about the period prior to the war which broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, nor about the propaganda that led up to that war. It was a period of heightening national tensions, boosting national tensions, which would quickly lead to their explosion. The time I'm referring to is the year 1991. With your permission, Your Honours, and with the assistance of the usher, I should like to show you an example of such propaganda. On the ELMO, please. We see here the cover page of a pro-Muslim, high-circulation magazine called Novi Vox, published in the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo, dated 1991. I think the date in the upper right-hand corner can be discerned. It says "Listopad," or "October." This purports to be a joke. The newspaper, which had its headquarters in Dobrovoljacka street, where, as the introduction to the war, units of the Yugoslav People's Army were massacred, even though those units were in agreement with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic withdrawing from the barracks. They were massacred by Muslim paramilitary formations. On this cover page we see a drawing of a Muslim soldier with a fez on his head, trampling severed heads of Serb leaders Karadzic, Koljevic, and others. So let me repeat. This was October 1991. This magazine was published on a regular basis, with the full permission of the authorities Sarajevo. To the left of the soldier we see the words "The Handzar Division stands ready," ready with an arm raised as in the Heil Hitler greeting. And this was the greeting used by the Ustashas, the shock units of the Nazi entity which was called the Independent State of Croatia during the Second World War. The Handzar is a kind of Oriental long dagger which this division used abundantly, and the Handzar was an infamous Ustasha Division composed exclusively of Muslims. It should not be forgotten that the notorious Ustasha camp called Jasenovac, in which at least 500.000 Serbs were killed during the Second World War, in most cases by slaughtering, that this camp was only 30 kilometres from Prijedor. Such a background necessarily provoked great fear and the instinct for self-preservation among the Serbs of Prijedor. To the right of the Muslim soldier are the words, "The Fourth Reich is coming, Willkomen," or "Welcome." "I am an Ustasha. I am an Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting my colleague and the Court, but I was concerned about one comment that cannot be reflected or corrected on the record absent my saying something, and I'm looking to see a description of the activity performed by this person on the cover of this magazine, and my colleague indicated, on line 22, page 15, "We see to the left of the soldier of the Handzar Division ready, an arm raised." I think the reference was to a possible Nazi-type stance. I do not see such an arm raised, and I'm wondering if perhaps either I'm missing something or it could be pointed out, or if it's just perhaps a mistake by counsel, he could correct the record. Thank you. Again, I apologise, but I found it quite an obvious error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Stojanovic, it's true that we do not see that on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't following the transcript, I was looking at the picture, and I didn't notice how it was translated. I didn't say that the hand was raised, but I was saying that the Ustasha greeting was identical to the Nazi greeting, but instead of the words "Heil Hitler," they used the word "ready" or "for the home ready," with a hand raised. In this case the hand is not raised, but the greeting "ready" is a Nazi Ustasha greeting which is regularly accompanied by the raising of the hand, but I didn't say that the hand was raised on this picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. In which case I assume Mr. Stojanovic is correcting his comment on line 22 where he said "to the left of the soldier, an arm raised." That is incorrect then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I do correct the transcript because that is not what I meant. Of course the hand isn't raised, it is lowered, but my explanation was that the words "ready" is accompanied by the raising of the hand, similarly as in Nazi Germany. Sometimes they don't have to raise the hand. Sometimes they say, "Heil Hitler," without raising the hand. So I accept that the transcript needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, perhaps you could go further and more quickly over this area and go on to your defence of your client Mr. Zigic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Only a few more words about this picture. "'I'm an Ustasha. I'm an Ustasha,' Slavko Ecimovic cried out. The leader of the assault on Prijedor that took place on the 30th of May, 1992." Even in Omarska, as we were told by a Prosecution witness, Azedin Oklopcic, during the proceedings on the 15th of May 2000. Could this picture now be removed from the ELMO, please. I apologise, Your Honour, we're just checking the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for my knowledge, did -- was "Ustasha" exactly corresponding to Croat or to Muslim or to both?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, members of the Ustasha movement were predominantly Croats, but a segment of the Muslims joined the movement. Others segments of the Muslim population joined the partisan movement and the communists. So Muslims could be found on all sides. But this segment that joined the Ustasha movement through this Handzar Division had the worst possible reputation, and this was a smaller section of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Political decisions reflected in style this propaganda. Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of three constituent nations, the Muslims or Bosniaks, the Serbs, and Croats, as is stated in the Constitution of that republic. Consensus of all three constituent nations needs to be achieved for all the most important decisions. However, the Muslim-Croat coalition led by nationalistic parties interpreted the Constitution as a card game preference where -- which is always played in threes, with the aim of two defeating the third. In accordance with such an interpretation of the Constitution, they would say to the third ethnicity, "By our order and contrary to your will, you will no longer be what you are and what you want to be, that is, Yugoslavs, even if you were born as such." Furthermore, they would say, "You, the Serbs, contrary to your will, will have to accept as your president a person who in his work called the Islamic declaration issued as long ago as 1975, declared, and I quote, 'There can be no peace or coexistence between Islam and non-Islamic societies and political institutions,'" due to which, as a Muslim fundamentalist, he spent ten years in gaol. Of course, I'm referring to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Your Honours, try to put yourself in the position of those unfortunate people and think what option you could possibly choose, at least the vast majority of that people, within such a political and historical context. In a certain sense, even the Dayton Agreement acknowledged the legitimacy of these decisions of the Serb people. The war that preceded Dayton was led by two camps: a camp which during the war was absolutely against the solutions provided for by the Dayton Agreement - that is, they favoured a unity with Bosnia-Herzegovina - and those who accepted the Dayton Agreements as the fulfilment of their minimum requirements, that is, the Serbs. That means that the rights and objectives were denied to the Serbs which were acknowledged by the Dayton agreements. Your Honours, allow me to repeat, with your permission, that the purpose of this part of my statement should not, under any circumstances, encourage inter-ethnic passions, but that I refer to these political and historical facts merely because of their impact on the possible existence of the act -- of the crime of persecution. That is why it is important to say a few more words about the persecutions within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, about which the Prosecution has provided you a one-sided and simplified picture. Extensive information about this can be provided in an article by a qualified expert and member of the administration of the former US president George Bush Sr., Mr. George Kenney, in his article entitled "Take off the Blinders on Bosnia," published in the Los Angeles Times of the 5th of June, 1997. From this article, it can be seen that, judging by the number of refugees, that the most persecuted people in Bosnia were the Serb people. We should like to tender this article as our exhibit, and I think the number would be D6/4. I have a sufficient number of copies for the Trial Chamber. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state consisting of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The capital of that state is Sarajevo, and Sarajevo is at the same time the capital of the part of the country called Bosnia. Before the war, there were more than 150.000 Serbs in that town. Now they are not there any more; only a couple of thousand remain since the war. The capital of Herzegovina is Mostar, in which one-third consisted of each of the three ethnic groups. It was the centre of Serb culture and commerce. Before the war, there were almost 35.000 Serbs there; after the war, only 400. Well, where are the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina? The capital of Herzegovina was more thoroughly cleansed than all others, and prior to all others. However, that is not something that the Trial Chamber will learn from the Prosecution, just as it will not learn about the camps for Serbs in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Dretelj, which was founded on the 4th of April, 1992, the survivors of which could be counted on the fingers of our hands. We can learn a little from the case of the Celebici camp on the territory of Konjic municipality, where, out of 7.700 Serbs prior to the war, one year into the war only 280 remained. An interesting piece of information is also the fact that the Celebici camp was established a little earlier than all the other camps on the territory of Prijedor municipality and that it existed until the very end of 1992. Migrations of this kind necessarily had to result in the resettlement of Serbs in other areas and the arrival of members of other ethnic groups to take their place, who in their turn had to leave their homes in other parts of the same state. The persecutions of some in these cases necessarily bring pressure to bear on members of the persecuting people to areas where the persecuted are more powerful. In most cases, this is not revenge but simply the quest for shelter, for mere survival, and for protection for one's family and a roof over one's head. The town closest to Prijedor is Sanski Most, which is only some 30 kilometres away. Before the war, the Serbs constituted the majority. After the war, only a couple of per cent of Serbs remain; the rest are Muslims. Where did those Muslims now come from, and why are there no more Serbs there? A part of the answer to that question would be provided when answering the question as to what happened with the population as a whole in the area. However, from the legal point of view, our main submission here is that every conflict of this kind, especially an armed conflict, contains in it per definitio persecution; by definition, in other words, contains persecution. There is no such conflict that does not contain persecutions, and these become more and more pronounced as civilian objectives are proclaimed to be legitimate military objectives. That is why the Defence will insist upon the legal definition of persecution and a concept that will be distinct from elements which are characteristic of any armed conflict. Closely connected to what has been said above is the quest for the reasons for the formation of investigation centres or, as some call them, camps. In the submission of the Defence, there are far more arguments in favour of believing that the investigation centres or camps were the product of the events of the 30th of May and not of the 30th of April, 1992. Therefore, it is our submission that there is more reason to believe that the main cause for their formation was the attack on Prijedor and not the Serb takeover of power. Certainly, it cannot be said that the Serb takeover of power in Prijedor was legal, but with regard to its legitimacy, we might even refer to the Dayton Agreement. What is most important is that it was carried out through the organisation of the highest representatives of the Serb authorities in Prijedor and without any bloodshed. Furthermore, the authorities in Sarajevo, devoid of Serb representatives at the time, had lost their legitimacy. On the other hand, the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992 was neither legal nor legitimate. It was led by Slavko Ecimovic, who was a declared Ustasha, and with the wholehearted assistance of Ismet Mesic, the Hadzija, the boss of the local underground. It provoked many casualties, dozens of dead, far more wounded, and a great deal of devastation. The mentioned attack on Prijedor was not backed by the authorities in Sarajevo, as Witness Azedin Oklopcic alleges, testifying here on the 15th of May, 2000. Finally, as can be seen from Prosecution exhibit, by decision of the chief of the security centre, Simo Drljaca, the Omarska investigation centre was in actual fact established in response to this attack on the 31st of May, 1992, and it is from then on that detainees were brought en masse to Omarska and Keraterm. Your Honours, the accused Zoran Zigic found himself in the midst of this wartime whirlwind, a man who prior to the war did not have any serious criminal record but who lived in the fast lane, partly also linked to the occupations he engaged in. For a time he was a musician, but he was also a driver and a taxi driver. In fact, he led a kind of bohemian life. On the other hand, this life prompted many rumours, a great deal of gossip and tales in a provincial environment such as Prijedor was, especially as, by his beliefs of a modern young man, stood apart from his provincial surroundings. Unfortunately, the life he led led him to a passion that we would call a disease, which led him to develop a split personality. What we are referring to is excessive consumption of alcohol but also the use of soft drugs. The war exacerbated all this, which is only logical and only to be expected among individuals with such predispositions. This is confirmed by the expert findings of two German psychiatrists, which we shall certainly be tendering into evidence, but also quite a number of Prosecution witnesses have spoken to that effect. And those were the causes of his excesses, rather than any politics, ideology, or intolerance towards members of other ethnicities. Zoran Zigic had no interest in politics and he was never a member of any political party, and there were very few people in former Yugoslavia who were never members of any political parties. In particular, he was never a member of the SDS. To corroborate that, we tender certificate number 01/99, dated the 12th of January, 1999, and we should like to tender it into evidence as our Exhibit D7/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would ask for a moment to voice its objection. In the clear language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for a moment, let me wait for the translation. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The clear language of Rule 84 indicates that: "Before presentation of evidence by the Prosecutor, each party may make an opening statement. The Defence may, however, elect to make its statement after the conclusion of the Prosecution's presentation of evidence and before the presentation of evidence for the Defence." Therefore, this is an inappropriate and impermissible time for evidence to be submitted. If, in fact, at a later time, through a witness, the Defence wishes to do so, the Prosecution would at that time reconsider, but it objects to any evidence being introduced during opening statement, according to the plain language of the Rule. Thank you. This, of course, Your Honour, would cover the article that was submitted by Mr. Kenney as well. We were going to wait until the end of the statement, but because it is a continuing violation of the Rule, we thought it appropriate to tell the Chamber our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that we interpret the Rules quite differently, and we feel that the Rules allow us to make these -- to submit this evidence. We see no obstacle to us tendering exhibits at this stage. Perhaps Ms. Somers feels we should call Mr. George Kenney and then, through him, tender his article. Or should we do it through a statement from a witness from Prijedor? Similarly, as Zigic will not be testifying, we will not have the opportunity to provide this certificate of the SDS through his testimony. In my personal opinion, every exhibit, with full respect to the other party, and giving an opportunity to the other side to have access to it, can be submitted to the Court. At any stage, it is up to the Court to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, but as you know, this is not really the time to give the other party a chance to state their position. This is an opening statement. It is a statement which cannot be disputed at this stage, or challenged. So you see, Mr. Stojanovic, this is an opening statement. It is not an occasion for exchanges with the other party. So maybe you should wait and tender these documents later on. In any event, please continue and we'll see at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something. I assume there is no problem in Mr. Stojanovic referring to these because Mr. Niemann referred to hundreds of documents in his opening statement, or at least dozens and dozens and dozens. You may be correct that they should be tendered formally at a later point, but I just wanted to clarify that he's certainly free, on the basis of precedent, to refer to the fact that we will submit or it will be tendered to work it into his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour Judge Wald --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify it. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- opening statement. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald, for reminding us of this. I also had that in mind. But in any event, please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. We are under pressure to hear your evidence. So the opening statement is a kind of practical framework. That is how I understand it, to set the framework for the presentation of your case. How much more time do you need to complete your statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think another 30 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. minutes on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should now have a break, then, because we have been working for an hour and a half. I was hoping you would finish before the break. We have to make the best use of the time. I hope you will not ask for an extension of time later on. So make the best of your time, please. We're now going to have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Stojanovic, please continue with your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again, Your Honours. I shall do my best to speed things up, but after all, it is a rather complex text which involves added effort on the part of our interpreters, so that is why I went rather more slowly, and I think another 15 or 20 minutes will bring me to the end of the statement. I was talking about Mr. Zoran Zigic's personality, and allow me to continue. When he was intoxicated, he made excesses and this brought him enemies. However, these instances of excessive behaviour were engaged in entirely independently of the ethnicity of the persons he came into conflict with and even regardless of whether it was wartime or peacetime. Everything depended on the alcohol intake. Alcohol, as the cause of the excesses, was more dominant than any other cause. That that is so can be seen from the excess which brought Zigic to the prison in Banja Luka in 1993. And before the judgement became effective in the courts in Banja Luka, he requested that he be transferred to The Hague and be tried on the indictments of this Tribunal. He committed a serious crime against members of the Serb ethnicity without any motives or reasons and not even remembering what he had done and what had actually happened. As I have said, it so happens that the Serbs were perhaps the most frequent victims of these excesses of his, but those excesses against Serbs were not described here, and what makes things even worse, they were at times misrepresented before this Tribunal. It was thus that it was not infrequent that Zigic should start a quarrel, start to shout, insult, and swear, and even to beat persons of Serb ethnicity but also of other ethnicities who happened to be in Keraterm on some sort of business but not as detainees. It is within this group that his conflict with Zivko Knezevic could be put, him being one of the chiefs of Keraterm who prohibited any food being brought to the detainees, to which Zigic reacted in a very stormy manner. However, when talking about such cases, the comments of Prosecution witnesses always was, and I quote, "Zigic is again insulting and beating detainees." Even his private family relationships have been interpreted as war crimes on his part. That is how his family relationship with his kum, Hasan Karabasic, in Trnopolje, was interpreted, and terribly exaggerated, even though Prosecution witnesses themselves say that while his kum was detained in Keraterm prior to this incident, Zigic looked after him and provided him with parcels. One of the important character traits of Zigic in those days was that somebody's superiority over him meant nothing to him, and he himself did not enjoy being superior to anyone else. So he didn't like anyone to have authority over him, but neither did he seek to have authority over others. This is a trait that is, in principle, completely out of character for war criminals. The Defence has pointed out on a number of occasions that on the 29th of May, 1992, Zigic was seriously injured, and much more will be said about this injury by our expert witness, Dr. Mirko Barudzija. The injury, which resulted in an amputation of part of his index finger on his left hand, necessarily significantly affected several aspects of relevance for this case. First of all, for a long time, Zigic could not beat anyone with that hand, and should he exert any major effort with other parts of the body, the injury caused pain. Secondly, the psychological affects on Zigic, because he had lost his left index finger, bearing in mind in particular the fact that he had earned his living as a guitar player, were very significant for a long time. Finally, that injury was a very visible identification element of Zigic, and in that connection it can be seen that many Prosecution witnesses made a crucial error when they allegedly identified Zigic during the commission of a crime. Dr. Barudzija will, together with the appropriate medical documents, testify to the fact that Zigic acquired his scar on his chin on the 19th of August, 1992, so that the Prosecution will have to explain how several witnesses that they have called and whose testimony we have heard claim that they recognised Zigic committing acts in June and July 1992 by his typical scar on his chin. We have said that the use of narcotics by Zigic turned him into a split personality. We have already described one aspect of that personality. However, when sober, he was generous towards everyone, without expecting anything in return, again, regardless of the ethnic background of those persons, both during the war and in peacetime. He would give food, cigarettes, and everything else he had, paying little attention to their value and his own needs. This other aspect of Zigic's personality was described slightly by one or two Prosecution witnesses, but Defence witnesses will say much more. Your Honours, since 1993, that is, from the time Zoran Zigic was taken into custody, he has not been drinking or taking drugs. You have had occasion to hear from Prosecution witnesses descriptions about a certain personality, or one side of that personality, and it is based on those statements that the indictment was compiled. You now have before you a different personality in the same person whom you are to judge, a personality who is willing to cooperate and one that can be reintegrated into society as stated by distinguished expert psychiatrists from Germany who have been engaged by the Registry of this Tribunal. However, Your Honours, the story about Zigic's personality is not a plea for mercy but a plea for justice and truth, and we are convinced that we will be able to show the truth, and that is that Zigic did not persecute non-Serbs, that he did not commit murders, and that he did not commit many of the other crimes which he is accused of in the indictment. However, a court is not addressed with pleas for justice and truth; it is what is expected of the court. However, Zigic's case is so complex that, in our opinion, it seems to us to really require extraordinary attention, effort, and understanding. I sincerely hope that in the presentation of its case, the Defence will assist the Trial Chamber to acquire a broader factual background and more legal alternatives and thereby provide the Chamber what is expected of it. The obligations of the Defence team in relation to the Trial Chamber have to contribute to a just and fair decision being taken. Your Honours, allow me to leave an argument or two for my closing statement. So with your permission, I would end my opening statement there. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. And now what is next?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we should now like to call our first witness, and that is Mrs. Soka Sikic. And with your permission, I would request that my colleague Mr. Deretic assist me in the continuation of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. I have a question, but I see Ms. Susan Somers on her feet, so I'm going to give her the floor first. You have the floor, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to confirm the pronunciation of the witness's name. Is it Sikic or Zigic? It's important for us because we follow the spelling of Sikic. Could you confirm that, please? If I could ask the Court to confirm the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the name is Sikic. I was using the computer in the Defence room, and I couldn't find the letter "sh," which is pronounced as s-h. "Sh," Sikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, may I have just a comment on your illustration of the common purpose, and just a friendly comment. You said that perhaps the common purpose of the whole people working here, the Defence, the Prosecution, the others, would be to take the money of the United Nations. Perhaps you add to it "to see to it that the justice is being done." That would be the primary common purpose. And suppose your common purpose is the right one, the vague one. It is not a criminal common purpose, after all. We are here considering criminal common purpose. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Stojanovic, I see on your list of witnesses the name is Sikic Soka. I see that name. And another question that I have for you, I thought that you or the accused wanted to make a statement. I had the impression that he wanted to make a statement. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are quite right. For a moment I omitted to mention it, but that was one of the things that I thought of prior to my opening statement. We would like the accused to make a statement. It is up to the Chamber to decide. We received an objection on the part of the opposing party against it, and with your indulgence, allow me to give a few arguments in favour of this statement which I consider would be useful. The Prosecution feels that, if I translated the word properly, it would be ridiculing the proceedings in court. However, in our submission, it would be quite the opposite. In August 2000, Zigic made a statement to psychiatrists, expert witnesses designated by the Registry, and who informed him that they were not obliged to keep confidential what he told them. Zigic did confess to some minor acts which he is charged with. After that, Mr. Zigic's Defence team requested that this expert witness finding with these admissions be admitted into evidence. In doing so, Zigic acted fairly, in our opinion. On the other hand, for more than a year now in this courtroom, we have been looking at Mr. Zigic. Why not hear his voice as well and some opinions of his? I believe that this would provide a better image to Your Honours of the person they have been looking at. The impression may be positive or negative. We would just like Your Honours to see and hear the person whose fate is being decided. The question of credibility of his statement is quite another matter. However, it is our opinion that there is no real difference between a statement by the accused given in this way and a statement of the accused as a witness who has made a not guilty plea. Whether the witness, as the accused, will incriminate himself and to what extent the Trial Chamber will base its judgement on the statement of the witness or the accused who pleads not guilty is up to the Trial Chamber. Mr. Zigic is aware that in the case of such statements, there is no cross-examination, but he also knows that the Trial Chamber may set the frameworks or the limits of what he can speak about, and he is ready to act within the confines of the framework set by the Trial Chamber. The way we interpret Rule 84 bis, unlike the Prosecution, the question of a solemn declaration being taken is not excluded. It just says that the accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration. So that we believe that it would be useful for the Trial Chamber to hear this witness to be able to assess his personality today. There is, however, a problem of a technical nature there. I fear that the spirit of that Rule indicates that this statement of his should be made at least at the beginning of our case, and this may perhaps upset the order of the presentation of evidence. So we would suggest that it take place during the time scheduled for his testimony or any other time prior to that should we have some room available or on our hands because a witness doesn't appear or for some other reason. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Susan Somers, there seem to be here at least two questions, that is, the possibility of making a statement and the properness of making such a statement, appropriateness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, last week the Prosecution gave in its submission on its position on when a Rule 84 bis statement, often referred to under other systems as a dock statement, is inappropriate by reading the language of Rule 84 and 84 bis. It is the position of the Prosecution that the application now by accused Zigic is out of time. It is not timely and is barred. The purpose behind an 84 bis statement is at the very earliest opportunity to narrow issues and that, by the language of 84 bis, at the latest, at the latest, would occur if the Defence for Zigic had deferred its opening statement, which it in fact did, then immediately after the opening statement of the Prosecution, which would be -- would have been February 2000. To allow accused Zigic now to have the benefit of manipulating a story based on over a year of testimony, and further attempting now, at the end of his own case, to manipulate his edition of facts, is not consistent with the purpose of the Rule, which we understand is a relatively common practice in European or continental jurisprudence, again with the purpose of early on narrowing issues. That is not the purpose of Zigic's attempt to get on the stand without cross-examination. His purpose now, which is clear from timing, having listed himself in two submissions as Witness 21 on his witness list, is that he finds it inconvenient to have to submit to cross-examination. Inconvenience is not what underlies this Rule. It would be effectively to gut the Rule of 84 bis to allow at this time that type of manoeuvre. It is, of course, true that indication of intent to testify, under 85(C), which it is the Prosecution's position is the only avenue open to Zigic now, having -- being outside of the time limits of 84 bis, an accused is always free not to proceed to take the stand, but that should not mean an automatic reversion to provision 84 bis, which has time limits which are set forth, as we've indicated in our submission, with some explanation by the -- I believe it was a commission or panel of experts, as to the purpose for the Rule. There has been no precedent for this type of untimely attempt to benefit from the statements of all their witnesses, and we think it would be a very risky endeavour at this point to deviate from the language of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, do you have a quick reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do have a response. I am speaking on behalf of Mr. Zigic, without the right of the Prosecution to cross-examine me. That is to say, I see nothing bad in that. I'm speaking exclusively in Zigic's favour. Why should Zigic not be allowed to say something? Of course, if Zigic abuses a fact by saying something afterwards, the Trial Chamber is highly qualified to assess this and to assess it as making his situation worse. It is our wish for the Trial Chamber to hear Zigic as they hear everybody else, although this may be an aggravating circumstance. And he might even bring up irrelevant factors, but I think that he only wishes to speak about his relationship towards the crimes he has been charged with, and I think that with that statement, we would not upset any of the rights of the Prosecution, nor would the Trial Chamber be placed in a position where, in a way, it changes any of its convictions. It is a matter of credibility, at all events, whether the Trial Chamber will attach any credibility or not to the statement that Mr. Zigic might make. But I do feel that it would help round off the picture painted as to the character of Mr. Zigic, and that is why we put the suggestion forward in the first place. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. The Judges will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, is Mr. Zigic ready to make a statement straight away, and if so, how long would he need for that statement? How long would it take? You may take a few moments to confer with your client, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to avail myself of that opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, and I thank the Court for its indulgence. As for the time that it would take Mr. Zigic, he thinks that one day would be required for his statement. But I don't think I have understood the provision, because it allows for the possibility of the Trial Chamber to set the frameworks of that examination. We should like to ask the Trial Chamber to enable this at some later date, but if that would mean that we would not have a chance of doing so at a later date, then perhaps it would be advisable for us to do it now, although we have witnesses waiting, they have been scheduled to appear this week, and I feel that we will have very little time to get through all the witnesses on our schedule for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, we repeat all of our foregoing objections, but we would indicate that should the Chamber, over our objection, permit an 84 bis statement to occur, it would be, in our opinion, an abuse by Mr. Zigic to be permitted to do so at the close of his case, inasmuch as that certainly -- that really flies in the face of the intention of the Rule. And if the Chamber does permit this type of statement to be given, over our objection, we would urge that it be done immediately under the strict control of the Chamber. Again, we feel the whole process is inappropriate, but should the Chamber make a decision otherwise, that it happen now, because I think it would really skew any value at a later time and really fly in the face of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning this issue, the Chamber renders the following decision: The Chamber notes that the accused Mr. Zigic proposed to testify as a witness at a given moment, point in time; at another point in time, the Defence stated that they would like to have the statement of the accused. According to Rule 84 bis, statement of the accused, the Chamber notes that Rule 84 bis provides for this possibility for the accused after the opening statement by the Prosecutor. But bearing in mind the specific features of this case, notably, the fact that we have five accused, there would be no sense in having the accused make a statement at a distant time, at a time removed. Therefore, each Defence counsel makes its opening statement before the presentation of evidence. Therefore, there is sense in having the statement of the accused as a continuation of the opening statement. In that sense, the Chamber accepts the facts that the accused Mr. Zigic may make a statement along the lines and in the sense of Rule 84 bis. And as the Rule states, the accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration and shall not be examined about the content of the statement. That is to say, the accused, from his point of view, has two opportunities of pronouncing himself. First of all, the opportunity within Rule 84 bis and the statement of the accused and the opportunity of appearing as witness within the frameworks of Rule 85(C): "If the accused so desires, the accused may appear as a witness in his or her own defence." So it may be done within the frameworks of Rule 84 bis and can also be presented as a witness, but it is up to us to discipline and organise this debate. But not within the sense of Rule 84 bis can he make this statement after the presentation of evidence has been produced. Therefore, Mr. Zigic can either make the statement now or he forfeits the right to make the statement. Taking note of the circumstances, the Chamber gives the accused Mr. Zigic the opportunity of making his statement under those provisions and with that proviso. What we are now going to do is to take a lunch break at this point. We adjourn for lunch, and this will give Mr. Zigic the right to prepare his statement, which cannot exceed 45 minutes. The Chamber also notes that once the accused Mr. Zigic is prepared to take the stand, he will be presenting some of his ideas, but we must also bear in mind the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fact that this statement is also covered by point (B) of Rule 84 bis, which states that: "The Trial Chamber shall decide on the probative value, if any, of the statement." That, therefore, is the ruling of the Trial Chamber. It has decided to give the accused Mr. Zigic the opportunity of making the statement based on the provisions of Rule 84 bis. We accord him a pause, which gives him time to prepare, and with the proviso that the statement of the accused does not exceed 45 minutes. That is the ruling of the Chamber, and having said that, we are going to take a 50-minute lunch break. We adjourn the hearing and return at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Stojanovic, we are going to proceed with the statement by the accused. We are of the opinion, as the text states, that as the accused did not make the solemn declaration, that that is to say, the accused shall make the declaration from where he is sitting. The other thing that I want to say is, of course, that the statement has as its basic framework and subject the indictment itself, so it cannot step outside the frameworks of the indictment. I should like to ask the usher, before we proceed, if the microphone of the accused Mr. Zigic can be switched on for Mr. Zigic to be able to make his statement. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do appreciate you taking this ruling and allowing us to proceed in this way. Mr. Zigic is ready to take the solemn declaration if need be before he goes ahead with his statement. He is ready to do so if you feel that that is what we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We mustn't mix things up, Mr. Stojanovic. Let us not mix up the issues. I think the Chamber is very clear. He is either going to make his statement in conformity with Rule 84 bis, which states: "The accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration and shall not be examined about the content of the statement." That is what the Rule states. And as I say, this is not something that I like to say with respect to the civil law system, the accused has always the right to lie. Now, we interpret this in the best possible way, of course, but it is up to Mr. Zigic to make his declaration under the terms that he sees fit, but as I say, with the only proviso that it be limited to the indictment, and that is why we have made the distinction of having the accused resume his place and not to go into the witness box and make his statement in the capacity of a witness and to take the solemn declaration. That is why we distinguished between the two positions. As you know, non-verbal communication is sometimes more -- is sometimes stronger than the verbal kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We accept certainly, Your Honours. The only dilemma is whether we will stay here and put questions to him or whether Mr. Zigic will speak himself. If we are asking questions, then it would be better, it seems to me, for us to go back to our original places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, I think I must make myself clear once again. There's no question. The accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration and shall not be examined about the content of the statement either by the Prosecution or by the Defence counsel or by the Judges, not even for clarifications. This is simply a statement. So if you wish to go back to your place, it's up to you. If not, Mr. Zigic will make his statement from his place. As you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Your Honour, we would go back to our seats, but with your permission, allow me to give him back his notes. Thank you very much. May we stay here after all? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems my colleague and I differ in our views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, the Rules do not specify where you have to sit, so it's up to you to choose. Regarding the statement, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 84 bis, I give the floor to the accused, Mr. Zigic. You have the floor. If you prefer to speak seated, you may do so. THE ACCUSED ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I would prefer to stand, out of respect for this Honourable Court. I should like to use some notes that I made and put on paper, and following your instructions, I will focus only on the points made in the indictment, so I will leave out much of what I intended to say about me personally - my work, my family, and so - otherwise I will not be able to fit into the time allotted to me. I spent most of my life outside my native town of Prijedor. For a time I worked in the Soviet Union and for a time in the Federal Republic of Germany, for a total of four or five years. For quite some time I worked in Zagreb in Croatia and also in Pula, which is also in Croatia, and for a time I lived and worked in Prijedor. I worked as a taxi driver and was a professional musician at the same time, and that is how I made my livelihood. Just before the beginning of the war, I fled from Pula, and I wouldn't like to go into the circumstances and tire this Chamber with the details. I arrived in Prijedor on the 31st of December, 1991, and until the 29th of April, 1992, I wasn't doing anything, actually. I had no job. I stayed in my parents' house, together with my wife and two children. On the 29th of April, 1992, I got my call-up papers. In the meantime, one could notice in town, a town I knew very well -- and I live on the outskirts of the town, but I spent most of my time in the centre of town and most of my friends were there. I didn't care whether they were Serbs, Muslims or Croats. That was quite unimportant to me. In fact, I had more Muslim friends than I did Serbs. That is no longer important. But tension could be felt in town, because I spent a lot of my time in cafes and restaurants. As I was a musician, this was normal. There was some intolerance, ethnic tension, verbal insults were exchanged, not physical yet, and I got the call-up on the 29th of April to report to the Prijedor police station number 1 centre. I was surprised, because I was a military conscript and I was never a reserve policeman. I was very surprised and I reported and was assigned to providing security for the SUP building. Throughout May, that is what I did, and the assignments were the usual security assignments for the SUP building itself. I had no other duties. During the armed conflicts in Kozarac on the 24th of May, I was part of the security forces of the Prijedor police station. I was aware, more or less, what was happening in the armed conflict. My native village, Balte, is right next to Kozarac, and it was normal that my family should be concerned. My father and mother were worried, and they sent me to visit the village to visit my relatives to see if they needed anything, if I could help them in any way. So I went. I went alone, using my own private car, and a couple of kilometres prior to arriving at my uncle's house I was attacked by a group of armed men. I didn't know who they were. Of course, I was very cautious and I resisted. I can quite frankly say I was afraid, and in that fear and haste -- I don't know how to explain it. I had in the vehicle a hand grenade, and as I was running short of ammunition, I used the hand grenade, but due to haste and fear and lack of caution, I injured and cut off the index finger on my left hand myself. In the meantime, some villagers from my village arrived, and they helped me repulse this attack by a group of armed people, who, I learned later, were Muslims from Kozarac. After that, I went back to Prijedor, together with my cousin, who took me to the hospital. I underwent surgery. I had to stay -- I was supposed to stay in hospital, but I refused, because in those days the hospital was extremely busy with more serious cases and I thought of myself as somebody with a light injury. I said I would stay home, I would be disciplined, I would come for regular treatment and therapy to the hospital. And that was the period when I refrained from taking any alcohol because of the medicines I was taking. However, nevertheless, sometimes I did have a drink, which had its consequences, so that I got an inflammation of the hand, and the 21st of May I had to go to hospital, where I stayed until the 26th of June -- I'm sorry, the 21st of June was the date. Then my finger was treated and the wound cleansed and I was discharged, and I wore bandages until the end of July, roughly. As regarding my stay in Keraterm, I was in Keraterm. I was a guard there. On the 2nd of June, 1992, my now deceased commander, Mirko Paras [phoen], rounded up the squad that was securing the SUP building and said that we no longer needed to do that but that he needed a unit to secure the Keraterm investigation centre. I have to be very sincere in addressing Your Honours and say that I didn't know that any such thing existed. But again to be frank, driving along the Banja Luka road on the 29th of May, I had to see Keraterm, and I did see it, and I saw a group of people at the gates to the Keraterm but I didn't know what it was about. On the 2nd of June, when we reached Keraterm, I found there a dreadful situation. That is the only word I can use for it. The first room in Keraterm, which the detainees called Room 1, maybe this was by chance, but it so happened that the people there were people I knew well in that room. Most of them were my friends. I can call them friends, not acquaintances. I found this very hard to bear. I do not wish to name those persons, but they were dear to me. I saw them lying on pallets, and we've heard evidence about that. I found that very difficult and hard to endure. I am a rather hot-blooded person, and I have a rather nasty tongue, as we say it, so I cursed, I swore. I didn't really care whether they were Serbs or Muslims or my colleagues from the police station. I simply had to let go of my feelings, and I did so by making a lot of noise and curses, and I would be prone to slap someone, whoever was close by, regardless of whether he was a Serb or a Muslim. I would be prone to do that. I did my best to spend as little time as possible in Keraterm. I can't say that the crimes that I heard referred to here happened - that is out of the question - but the very fact that they were there, how unkempt they were, the stench, it is something that no one can describe that hasn't experienced it, the stench of filth and unsanitary conditions. So I didn't spend much time there. I am an extremely emotional person, and I found it very hard to see my friends there, but I had no power to assist them except for giving some of them food, cigarettes, sometimes alcohol, too, as we were comrades in terms of drink as well. I spent ten days in Keraterm, not more. During that ten-day period and throughout that period, I didn't spend more than eight hours there because I spent very little time there. I would be there for 10, 20 minutes, sometimes an hour, and then go to the closest bar. Fortunately, right next to Keraterm there were a couple of bars, places where, anyway, I had spent most of my life. Since I was touched upon Keraterm, I should like to refer to the indictment in specific terms and counts from the indictment, and later on I would like to explain my position in relation to the indictment when I received it in 1996. I don't know exactly the number of the count charging me of brutal beating and killing a person called Sead Jusufagic, known as Car, and Emsud Bahonjic. I should like to tell this Honourable Trial Chamber, from the bottom of my soul, what actually happened on that occasion. I was horrified when I read some of the witness statements as well as the indictment. I am aware of such an event. I know that this happened to a person called -- known as Car and Bahonjic. I was present. The attack on the town of Prijedor took place on the 30th of May, 1992. Both these persons were captured during the attack on the town with weapons in their hands. Prosecution witnesses have confirmed that. The person known as Emsud Bahonjic is somebody I had never seen in my life. I don't know him. As for Sead Jusufagic, known as Car, he is somebody I knew very well. He comes from the town of Prijedor. He is a petty criminal who spent almost his entire life in gaol. Physically, he's very slight, not more than 40 kilos in weight, and according to information of inspectors who carried out an investigation with him, we were told, in an informal conversation, that this person, Sead Jusufagic, had a M53 machine-gun with which he had taken part in the attack on the town. I found that rather funny, because such weapons from the Second World War were almost as heavy as he was. At the same time, I was bitter because particularly in the area where he was active was the area where the largest number of Serb policemen and soldiers were killed. Looking at the event from the present-day perspective, I certainly wouldn't do that, what I did, but in that situation, as I was a participant in what was happening, I knew almost all the people who had lost their lives on that occasion, and even the Muslims who were killed, I knew most of them too, those that were killed during the attack. I didn't wish to take my revenge on Car. I wanted to humiliate him. I forced him. I emptied his machine-gun and ordered him to put it on his shoulder and to run round in a circle carrying it. I repeat, if this were to happen today after so many years, I wouldn't have done that, but at that time, that was how things were. And I feel deep remorse for doing what I did. But what happened later with Car will be shown through the Defence witnesses who were present at the event. While Car was running around in a circle, I myself don't know why - I was quite intoxicated - I hit him with my leg once. I kicked him, and that was all that I did to Car. I got on my motorcycle and left Keraterm to a bar. I don't know exactly which one, but I know I left. What later happened to Car, to be quite frank, I don't know, and I didn't know until I received the indictment. I didn't know that the man had been killed. As far as Emsud Bahonjic is concerned, as I have said, I didn't know the person, but I am aware of the incident in which he was involved. It occurred one day before or one day after this incident with Car. My acquaintance, Dusko Knezevic, who is also on the indictment, lost his brother, who was underaged, who was killed by his Muslim neighbours during combat activities in the area of Kozarac. The brother was 17 and a half. He was unarmed. His school friends caught him and cut him up and mutilated him with knives. He came to Keraterm to interrogate Muslims he knew regarding the circumstances of the death of his brother. I have to be quite frank and say that Dusko Knezevic, known as Duca, was extremely arrogant. Nobody could oppose him. And to be quite frank, I didn't even try to oppose him because I knew that he lost his brother and that he wanted to know who were the killers of his brother. Nobody opposed him, though there were a large number of people present, guards and other people who had come with Duca. He called out a number of people that he knew and the names he knew.
