I personally did not know any of them, though later on, I saw from the statement that a number of them from Kozarac, I still didn't know them. There was beating and curses and coercion. At one point, Duca hit with his truncheon a good friend of mine who was an Albanian by origin, Ismet, and I said to Duca, "Why are you hurting that man?" and then he hit me, too, with his truncheon. I was dumbfounded, and I didn't oppose him from then on. Then witnesses of the Prosecution mentioned this incident in which I did not participate, even though I was present. Regarding the count of the indictment charging me with the murder -- alleged murder of Mr. Drago Tokmadzic, I don't know that the man was killed, nor is there any evidence to prove that he was killed. I know Mr. Drago Tokmadzic very well, as a policeman. We would often have a drink together. And I must tell this Honourable Court that I always thought that he was a Serb. I never could conclude that he was of any other ethnicity. I'm still convinced that he's a Serb. However, from some Prosecution documents, I see that he's a Croat. I never saw Mr. Tokmadzic in Keraterm. Mr. Huse Ganic testified here in Court. He's a person I know extremely well. It was only here that I read his statement, because I didn't receive him in Banja Luka in 1996/1997. It was only when I came here that I read his statement, and I am horrified by the lies that it contains and the lies he repeated here in court. I should remind the Honourable Chamber that Mr. Huse Ganic expressed the wish to shake my hand, and I was ready to give him my hand after all those lies, but a misunderstanding occurred. In my gesture, I was trying to ask my attorney whether that was permissible, and His Honour the Presiding Judge thought from my gesture that I didn't want to shake hands. But that doesn't matter now. I was ready to shake hands with Huse Ganic, although he uttered some dreadful lies against me during his testimony. In Keraterm, as I have said, I stayed a maximum of ten days, a maximum of ten days. And my whole -- during the time I spent in Keraterm, I had terrible problems with my hand. I was suffering severe pain, and I had to take sedatives, painkillers, strong ones, but the circumstances were such that I was not able to control myself, and then I would also drink while taking these sedatives, which led to even more complications. During that period, sometime around the 10th of June - this was the 10th, and I think it was my last day in Keraterm because that's when I left - we were in the restaurant of the Oskar -- Oskar restaurant in Prijedor, a group of us, 10 or 15 of us, in fact. Most of them were my friends and acquaintances. Somebody spontaneously said that we should go to Omarska, to the Evropa restaurant to have lunch there. We accepted that proposal and went off. We went off in a minibus which was used in the investigation centre at Keraterm. The driver was Tomo Prodan. As I said, there were ten or fifteen of us. I can't give you the exact number, neither can I state the names of all the people. Some of the people I don't wish to name because there's no need to, and those who are on the indictment, that is not a secret to the Trial Chamber. They were with me. In the Evropa restaurant someone quite spontaneously brought up the question of the Omarska Investigation Centre and said that it existed. I did not know that it existed at all. That is to say, I had never seen the Omarska mine complex. I had never visited the mine complex before the war, and that was the first time, and I was surprised that anything like that existed in Omarska at all, because I had envisaged the Omarska mine in quite a different way. Not to take up too much time, let me say that we arrived in Omarska and one of my colleagues took me to the infamous "white house." In the second room on the left-hand side, I found a very dear friend of mine, Brkic Abdulah, who had been in Keraterm for a time, and he testified here as well and said that he thought that the two of us were friends, and let me take advantage of this opportunity to say that I too considered us to be friends. And upon the insistence of the Defence that he testify for the Defence, he changed his story the next day, the story he gave first, and then in his second version, he told a number of lies. I can't understand why he did this. I'm not going to blame anybody else; I'm just going to blame him, because he was the one that stated those lies, although in the first statement he made, 90 per cent of what he said was the truth, and all I wanted was for him to tell the truth. I talked to him, and at one point [redacted] was brought, and I always had every respect for him before the war, and I can say that during the war I respected him too and I have even more respect for him now, today. Some parts with regard to [redacted] -- I cannot say some things in respect to him because identities would be disclosed, and it is -- but it is important, if the Trial Chamber wants to hear something about this, then I would like to ask for a private session for a minute or two so I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one or two minutes of private session. Let us move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zigic, you may proceed. We are in open session. THE ACCUSED ZIGIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have also been accused of the killing of Mr. Becir Medunjanin in the indictment, and an individual under the nickname Hankin Ramic, Hankin. I know neither of those two individuals. I heard of them first of all when I encountered their names in the papers I got from the Prosecution. I don't know Mr. Becir Medunjanin's son Anes either, and therefore, understandably, I can't say anything about him, and this would disclose certain identities, and we can't lose time going into private session again. As far as the collection centre in Trnopolje is concerned, my lawyer, Mr. Stojanovic, explained the abuse of certain witnesses who testified here with respect to Mr. Hasan Karabasic. That was a man I liked. He is my kum, the kum to my family, and the kum to my uncle as well, my father's brother. I was very close to him while I was in Keraterm. I cared for him, I brought him food and cigarettes, and on one occasion, that is to say, the only occasion that I went to Trnopolje, I happened to meet Mr. Karabasic. And it is difficult for me to bring home to the Trial Chamber what happened, what kind of meeting we had. It was a meeting as if we met on the street. Not only did we -- at one point we hugged each other -- at one point he fell down and I extended an arm to help him. Now, some people had probably seen that and represented to the Trial Chamber that I had hit him, which is completely out of the question. I wanted my lawyers to reach Mr. Karabasic and to ask him to come here and testify, and in fact he was on our list at one point for witnesses, but unfortunately he is unaccessible and we don't know where he is at present, to clear that up. I should like now to focus about my knowledge on the indictment and the supporting material. I learnt of the indictment for the first time in 1995, but I didn't know the contents of the indictment. It was from the media that I learnt that I had been accused of war crimes and indicted by The Hague Tribunal. Through force of circumstance, I happened to meet Mr. Milan Vujin, who was the lawyer in the Tadic case and who came to visit me in the military detention in Banja Luka and expressed the desire for me to appear as a witness to testify for Mr. Tadic. I accepted doing so, but I had an informal conversation with him, and he brought the indictment along and gave it to me and the supporting material of a large number of witnesses. I had all this in Banja Luka. When I read the indictment itself and everything that I was being accused of and the counts against me, I was horrified, and when I read -- I had the -- and all the statements that I saw from the people, although they weren't my friends. I had never heard of those events taking place at all, let alone that I was the perpetrator. Then I gave serious thought to appearing before this Tribunal in order to prove the contrary. I was never afraid of the indictment. The indictment is a very serious one. I am accused of grievous, terrible crimes, but I was not afraid. I am not afraid today either. I am only sorry that I have limited time at my disposal, whereas I would like to say many, many things. But why I have taken this step is that I wish to avoid provocations by the Prosecution, because I have been listening to them now for three years and I am not ready psychologically for them. I'm still not psychologically ready to be able to contend with them. I skipped a portion with respect to the indictment and the time I spent -- that is to say, after I left Keraterm, because the indictment states that I was present on the 24th of July, during what I can freely call the massacre at Keraterm. On the 24th, that cannot be possible, because on the 24th of July I was in the courtyard of my parents' house with my very dear friends. I cannot say that we had gathered together for any happy celebration. We had gathered together to commemorate the death of my 21-year-old friend who had actually been killed that day, a lovely man, so that we sat there and we had quite a lot to drink. I went to bed and went to sleep, and I heard of the incident only the next day when I was in town in one of the bars that I frequented, because the town was -- tongues were wagging about the incident and what had happened. There is a lot that I could say with respect to my indictment; however, I don't have the time to do so. I could go into the details. I interpreted the Rule differently. I'm not a legal man myself, and I relied on the good offices of Mr. Stojanovic, who has a better understanding of the law. I thought that I would be asked questions by the Judges, by Your Honours, and I would be happy to assist the Trial Chamber to throw more light around the events relating to my indictment and the charges in it. But as I can see, that would be impossible, and so in the context of all this I fear that I have left something vital out, some important matter out. I'm sure that I probably have. All I can say, in general terms, is that I have every confidence in this Tribunal and in this Honourable Trial Chamber that they will bring in a just judgement. I do not want to skirt my responsibilities for the things that I am responsible for. I don't wish to say that I was a good man in 1992. I most certainly wasn't. I wasn't good to myself, and therefore, by the same token, I wasn't good to anyone else. And unfortunately, I can ascribe most of that to alcohol, but then it is my fault for bringing myself into that state. You know, sometimes one is not always able to control oneself. Something breaks in you. All those images, everything that happened, and looking at all the people that were very dear to me, I couldn't understand that -- for example, let me -- Mr. Brkic, for example, Brkic and I can be at other sides of the gun barrel. This was something that I could not have conceived of, and not only for Mr. Brkic, but for other people in Prijedor too, and I think that the people listening to me today share my opinion and views. Unfortunately, because of the few extremists on all three sides, these terrible conflicts occurred in our town. This Tribunal and the truth that has emerged before this Tribunal -- and that is why I have asked to be able to speak, I would like to be believed. I would like the Trial Chamber to believe me. I have no reason to lie. But I should also like to warn you, Your Honours, that I have heard some terrible, horrific lies from some Prosecution witnesses. The only thing I'm sorry about is that I won't have a chance of answering any questions that you might have with respect to the counts in the indictment. I made the firm decision to appear before this Tribunal and I had contacts with the government of the Republika Srpska and the deputy justice minister in 1996, and at the time the chief of police of the police station in Prijedor was still the late Mr. Drljaca. Mr. Drljaca opposed this. I know that by talking to Mr. Vujin. He said that he had terrible difficulties because Mr. Drljaca did not permit anybody to appear in the Tadic case as a witness who was from Prijedor. I don't know how the late Mr. Drljaca learnt that I was thinking of giving myself up, but I do know that they exerted great pressure on me. Inspectors from Prijedor came to see me, to caution me, to warn me, and say that I would only be able to go to The Hague dead, a dead man. But luckily, I was in a military investigation centre and therefore protected under the jurisdiction of the army, and I was relatively safe. My life was not in jeopardy; I can't say that it was. Through force of circumstance, Mr. Drljaca lost his life in the well-known events. I need not recount them here. And in 1997, at the end of 1997, I had a very serious conversation relating to giving myself up, my surrender, which took place in 1998. And I'm sure the President knows about this, because I have a piece of paper with your signature, Your Honour. You saw to my transfer from Banja Luka to The Hague. That paper was signed by you. Let me now say a few words about the period I spent in the UN Detention Centre. I must say quite frankly and openly, I can only say thank you to you, thank you to all the staff in the United Nations Detention Unit in Scheveningen. I cannot single out anybody, because all of them are generally good people. They're all professionals and we have been accepted there first of all as human beings. Nobody treats us as criminals or looks at us as criminals, and it has not been proved that we are criminals yet. We shall see which ones of us are criminals and who are not. I should also like to thank the registry, because they have enabled me to get married under these very specific and extraordinary circumstances. I did get married, and that is once again thanks to the organisation, to the registry, and the Tribunal, for allowing me to do so, and my wife is expecting a son. That is to say, my wife gave birth to a son on the 15th of September, as a result of the marriage, and I can say that I'm a very happy man in that respect. The isolation or semi-isolation from civilisation has had a great effect on me as a person in my thoughts and deliberations, and believe me, I have a lot of time for thought. I very often think back to the year 1992 and the events that took place in that year, and if everything were to be repeated and if I were to go back to my native town in 1992, I can't say that I would have fled, that I would have fled, but quite certainly I wouldn't have acted in the way I did. I would try to find my way about things, as many other people did. I would have perhaps driven a vehicle, tried to isolate myself from some of the direct events that took place and direct conflicts, or something of that kind. I had a great deal of time to think about all those things, so it is understandable that I'm able to come to that conclusion today after all that thought. Everything that happened in 1992, we have heard a lot about those events here from various witnesses, the events. I don't want to refer the witnesses as Prosecution witnesses or Defence witnesses. They were eyewitnesses, those people who were there. We have heard a lot of truth about the events, and it is painful. The truth is painful for all of us who come from that town and, of course, for me too. By taking this opportunity, as this is an open, public trial, I call upon all the citizens of Prijedor, the Muslims, if they consider that I have wronged them in any way, it is still not too late. They can come to this Honourable Tribunal and testify against Zoran Zigic if they feel fit to do so. I am quite calm and collected in saying that because I know that I never committed any major serious crimes. If this Trial Chamber does consider that I committed a crime, I will agree with the judgement. I will accept any judgement that this august Trial Chamber brings, because I personally believe that I did make mistakes. And even if I just slapped somebody, that was a mistake and a crime, too, under those conditions. On this occasion, the person that [redacted] exaggerated the event, but that, too, is understandable. [redacted], I should like to deeply apologise and hope that one day I will emerge from all that, that I will meet [redacted], and that I personally will be able to express my sincere remorse and repentance for the harm I did him. I think [redacted] was not in pain because [redacted] What hurt him was because he has a staunch character and his name is respected in our town and it was more the humiliation that pained him rather than the act itself, and I profoundly I apologise to him. I express my deep remorse and repentance to all who consider I wronged them in any way during the war. But I consider that I didn't -- that -- although the -- some of my gestures must have pained them. I thank this Honourable Trial Chamber and you, Mr. President, for having allowed me this brief time to stand up and make a statement of my own. If this Trial Chamber deems necessary, I am always ready to answer any questions frankly and openly. Thank you very much once again for giving me this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Zigic. Please be seated. As you know, we're not going to ask you any questions because that is the ruling. I did not wish to interrupt Mr. Zigic's statement, but I saw Ms. Susan Somers on her feet. So, Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, without going into any detail because we are in open session, I would ask that the appropriate redactions be made upon reviewing some of what was just said by Mr. Zigic. If the Chamber wishes to go for a second into private, I will indicate what needs redaction. Otherwise, I would ask for the opportunity to make sure that it does not go out without redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Sikic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, I can. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please approach the microphones and make yourself as comfortable as possible, and thank you very much for coming. You will first be answering questions by Mr. Deretic. You have the floor. Your witness, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to introduce yourself. Tell us your name and surname and the name of your father.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: My name is Soka Sikic. My father's name is Miro Rajlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of February, 1956, in the village of Podvidaca, Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What are you by occupation?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I'm a butcher, a trades -- salesperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I'm now living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have two children; a son of 23 and a daughter of 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what your ethnicity and religion is.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb by ethnicity, of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What about your husband?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: My husband is a Croat of Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I do know Zoran Zigic. I've known him since 1980, when we moved to the district where Zoran Zigic had been living from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you identify him in this room?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he's seated.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: To my left, over there, right facing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: I'm going too fast obviously.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I've known Zoran Zigic since 1980, when we moved to his area. We are very close neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he's married?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: That same year that we moved there, he married Milka Zigic. They had two children, Natasa and Sanja. And I also know that he has a second wife, Sanja, and a son called Nikola, and I know them all very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know his parents?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Savka and Nikola Zigic. I know them, and I adore them as elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, how far is your house from the Zigic's house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: About 50 metres away. You just cross a yard and you're there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us whether you had any contact before, during, and after the war with Zoran Zigic's parents?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were regularly in contact before the war, during the war, and now, ever since we moved to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Zoran Zigic was a member of the armed forces of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the war started in Prijedor and the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was Zoran wearing a uniform in those days?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did he have a cap on his head?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in that period, did you ever see Zoran Zigic with his hair dyed or wearing an earring in one or both ears?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you ever see him wearing black gloves with the fingers cut off?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I never noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What colour was Zigic's hair?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Dark, very dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, do you know when the Serbs took over power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992. At the end of April. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how this takeover took place? Was it by peaceful means or was there violence?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Mostly by peaceful means. Peaceful, peaceful. There was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Prijedor was attacked by Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: A month later. On the 30th of May, 1992. A month after the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you be kind enough to tell us what part of Prijedor you live or, rather, what part of Prijedor is your house and the Zigic house? What is the area referred to?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: It's called Cirkin Polje, in the direction of Mount Kozara, on the slopes overlooking Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what is the ethnic composition of the population in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Multiethnic. There were Croats and Muslims, but Serbs were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, do you know that Zoran Zigic was wounded during the war?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran wearing bandages on his left hand?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: That was after the attack on Prijedor, when he was wounded in his left hand. His finger was cut off, something like that, I think. And he was wounded for a second time on the 19th of August, again in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, for how long did you see Zoran walking around with his fist bandaged? Can you remember roughly? Can you answer that question for me?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think for quite a long time. In June, July, maybe even into August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that after the beginning of the war in the area of Prijedor municipality, you would see Zoran and have contact with him. Could you answer the following question: During that time period, could you feel any change of attitude by Zoran Zigic towards you and your husband as his neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, we could always look to him for protection should we need it, to him and his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you know of anyone in your neighbourhood in that time frame being mistreated by Zoran Zigic or abused or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, had you heard of the investigation or collection centres in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Which centres were they?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when these investigation centres were set up?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think after the attack on Prijedor, the days that followed, two or three, five days after that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was taken into custody in those investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think the people who did not respect the Serb authorities and who participated in any way in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, after Prijedor was attacked, that is, on the 30th of May, 1992, do you know whether anyone from your neighbourhood ended up in one of those investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Why? Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. Nobody hurt us or the other neighbours of other ethnicities and probably they hadn't taken part in the attack or had no ill intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Ms. Sikic, do you have any knowledge about the fact that in Keraterm a large number of people were killed in one night?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that event occurred?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: It occurred towards the end of July, I think. I think it was the weekend, the night between the Friday and the Saturday, between the 24th and the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly where you were that day or, rather, that evening?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I can because, even before, we had always socialised with Zoran Zigic and his family, and that night we were also together in front of their house. We came, my husband and I. He was at home. We arrived around 2000 hours. There was some of Zoran's friends there already; his wife; his children; his mother and father, Savka and Nikola. We sat around for a while. We started a barbecue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you know all those people who came that evening?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Not all of his friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether anyone was playing that night among the people sitting in the Zigic garden?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two young men were playing and Zoran as well, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could I ask for a private session for a couple of minutes because of two or three questions that I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about that evening. You said it was a Friday, the 24th.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How did the people get together? Did they come individually or all of them at once?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't all come at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When did the company get together? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: About 2200 hours. It was already night-time when we had all congregated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that you arrived about 2000 hours with your husband. Was Zoran Zigic already in the garden?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In what condition was he? Can you remember that particular detail?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He was rather drunk already. He was gay. He was playing. He was making a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when the company was fully formed in that garden?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I said about 2200 hours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After that, what happened? Did you continue all together in the garden?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We sat around. We were drinking as usual, having a barbecue, playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the period from 2000 to 2200 hours, was Zoran in the yard with you throughout?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He wasn't, because we weren't there all the time either. Our house was close by. We would go home to bring something, to see how our children were. So Zoran, too, would go to bring bread, drinks. So as the company increased, we needed more and more stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After 2200 hours, what happened or, rather, was Zoran with you in the garden throughout?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was there until just before midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, by then he was really drunk, and he went to sleep it off. My husband took him to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears from where I'm sitting that this witness has a piece of paper in front of her with some notes from which she is reading as she's answering these questions, and at the very least, the Prosecution would like to see the contents of these notes. We would like to know where they arose from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I know, the witness probably made notes herself. I don't know what it is. Perhaps the best thing would be to ask the witness. I can't see from here that the witness has anything in front of her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain? I just have some dates written down here to remind me because it was a long time ago. So one forgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you be so kind enough to show my learned friend and Their Honours, because I can't really see from here what you have in front of you. The usher --

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I can show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps the simplest thing, Your Honour, would be if the counsel for Mr. Zigic would simply agree to make a copy of these notes available to the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be permitted, Mr. President, I too would like to see what it is. I would like to see the notes. Could I ask the usher to show the notes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These notes are in the B/C/S language. It might be simplest if we could simply have a copy and try to translate them at some later date. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all I can say, these are just a couple of dates. I know that Ms. Sikic was brought here about 10.00, and I know that other witnesses have also used notes. So in view of the suggestion of the Prosecution, we will be guided by your ruling, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, did you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. It seems to us that there appears to be a lot more information than just a couple of dates on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, I think, to make things quite clear, since you are ready to provide these notes, I think it will be a good idea to have a copy and a translation so there should be no doubts. I think these are clearly notes to assist the witness but, even then, that should not be a problem. We could just tender a copy and have it translated for the parties. Do you agree, Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. I really don't see any problem. But I have to observe that witnesses hitherto have been using similar notes, on the one hand; on the other, there are really a large number of facts that occurred a long time ago, and in that context I assume that the witness made these notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think we agree, Mr. Deretic. That was the suggestion of the Chamber. The problem that arises is, as you understand, the notes were written in a language which the other party cannot understand. If it was the same language, it could be inspected and that would be the end of it, but because it is in a different language, it would not be necessary to have it translated if one could understand immediately. So this is the only reason why we are ruling that it should be tendered and translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is fine. Mr. Zigic's Defence is not making any objections in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue with the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to repeat your answer to my question: Where and when and why did Zoran Zigic leave the yard?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Because he was quite drunk and he was drowsy, and so both he and we wanted him to go and lie down, and just before midnight he went into his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he went to sleep?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: On a couch in the kitchen. He lay down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: My husband took him there, and when he came back, he said that he was lying down and that he had put his pistol under the pillow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, when you arrived at Zigic's yard, did you hear any shooting?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: As there was a war on, one could hear shooting, but far and wide between.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell me: After Zoran went to sleep, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: We stayed behind, sitting around in the same way as when Zoran was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: After that time period, did you hear some shooting which was coming from the direction of the town?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. After midnight the shooting started, shooting of great intensity, something we had not yet become accustomed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were there any comments made among your company regarding the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We were all surprised, and I can't remember now whether anything in particular was said. I remember that there was shooting, which we were not really happy about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What was the intensity of the shooting? Did it last? Was it continuous or individual shots, or how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, the shooting went on for two or three hours, but again, in bursts of fire, then a pause, then it would intensify. It went on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you a similar question. Amongst you, did you make any comments about the shooting, in the sense that it differed in intensity from the shooting you had heard on earlier evenings?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were all wondering what was going on. Nobody knew what it was. I think somebody said, "There goes mad Ziga shooting again," but I don't remember who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When did you go home? When did you leave the Zigic's yard?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: After 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did your husband leave the Zigic's yard with you?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: The two of you, did you go straight home to your own house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In view of the intensity of the shooting, did you know where it was going on or what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We just saw that it was coming from the direction of the town, but we didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: The next day, in the morning, did you learn anything more about the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I was working, and my job was close to my house, and I kept on working in spite of the war, my husband stayed behind and he went to town, and he heard in town and I heard at work from customers that quite a large number of people had been killed. There was this story being spread in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where were these people killed?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: In Keraterm, as that was the closest collection centre to where we were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: The Zigic's yard, how far was it from the centre of town and from Keraterm itself?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: It is on an elevation, on some high ground in relation to town, in the direction of Mount Kozara. It is a hill. Right across the way is the airport. So we are on a higher ground than the town, and Keraterm is to the left of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, as the crow flies, what would the distance be from Keraterm to the Zigic yard?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Maybe 700, 800 metres. I don't believe it is a kilometre as the crow flies; less than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After this event that took place in Keraterm, do you know whether the incident was discussed in town and what was being said about it, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, except that quite a number of people were killed. I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony you said that Zigic was wounded on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us when Zoran was wounded for the second time and what you know about the incident.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He was wounded for the second time on the 19th of August, and I know that extremely well because on that day my son, who was a miner, was with him. And I mention that date as a day I celebrate. I call my friends, my kums and neighbours to lunch. Because when Zoran was wounded in the chin, the bullet passed through the body of his car. My son cried, thinking that Zoran was killed. I was at work when Zoran took the car. My son was in front of the garage, and he loved Zoran, adored him, and he could always go to see him and he loved to accompany him, to go fishing, and in fact Zoran taught him to eat fish and cheese when he was small. So without a second thought, he got into the car and went with Zoran. And relations with Zoran were such that he could always use our car, without any questions being asked. However, it was wartime. How things happened exactly, I don't know. Anyway, he was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, some witnesses here said that on that occasion your son had been kidnapped by Zoran. What can you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, and I can claim that with absolute certainty. Our son could go with him whenever he wanted, wherever he wanted, and Zoran could use the car as if it was his own, and he would always bring it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Two more questions for you. Until this second wounding, did Zoran Zigic have a scar on his chin?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And one final question for you. How would you, let us say, as the next-door neighbour, describe Zoran Zigic's personality in a few sentences?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know Zoran - we always socialised, went to excursions together, had barbecues together before the war - I could always look to him for any protection if I needed it. When he drinks, he's a bit difficult, but again, he hurts himself most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Talking about ethnic relations, did you ever sense any kind of hostility? What kind of relationship did he have with your husband Ivica?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What about other neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think he never had any disputes with anyone in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That ends my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Deretic. I should like to confer with my colleagues concerning an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, how much time do you need for your cross-examination? The entire time used by the examination-in-chief or less? Of course, you can't use more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I would ask for about 35 minutes, which would have us finished at about 5 minutes after 3.00, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I think that the best way to proceed is to prolong our session by half an hour. That is to say, let us take a break now, reconvene to finish the witness today, which means we'll be working a little late. Madam Registrar, is there any apparent inconvenience in that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently I do not think that this causes any trouble if we do take a brief break now to allow the interpreters to have a short rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we're going to have a 25-minute break, after which we shall reconvene for the cross-examination and try to get through this witness by the end of the day. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it be possible, Your Honour, during this break, if we could look at the notes that the witness has in front of her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes. Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already stated my views with respect to the question raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us adjourn, and then you can discuss the matter. A 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Mr. Saxon, you have the floor for the cross-examination. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has managed to produce a very rough translation of the notes that the witness had in front of her during the direct examination, and we have made copies of this very rough translation. If the Trial Chamber would like, we could provide copies of this rough English translation to the Trial Chamber, subject to, of course, a final translation being done to these notes. It's up to the Trial Chamber if they would like to see this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I said Sokic. I mean Sikic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When did you write these notes?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Here in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at about noon, after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you alone when you wrote these notes or were you with someone at that time?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I was in the room. I was sitting at the table. My husband was lying down on the bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you what to put in these notes at any time?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No. I knew that I had to know when the attack on Prijedor took place, when the takeover of power took place, and a long time has passed since then. So instead of doing guesswork, I jotted this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, did Zoran Zigic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, except for Ziga, Zoran Zigic, known as Ziga.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ziga. So to understand your testimony, on the 24th to 25th of July, that night or early morning when a lot of shooting was heard and neighbours said, "There goes mad Ziga shooting again," were they referring to Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Zoran Zigic have a reputation for shooting his gun a lot?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To what do you ascribe then the comments of those neighbours, "There's goes mad Ziga shooting again"?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said. Whatever happened, when he had been drinking, he would start shooting and shouting and making a general noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned during your direct testimony that when Mr. Zigic drank, he became a bit difficult. Would you describe Mr. Zigic, in 1992, as an alcoholic?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't always drunk, but he liked drinking, and it was wartime, after all, and you behaved the way you did with anything that was at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During June, July, August of 1992, would you often see Mr. Zigic armed with a firearm?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He would usually carry a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In fact, as you mentioned earlier, he was trusted to go to sleep with that pistol under his pillow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: That's what happened when he lay down, but I don't know if he usually went to bed with his pistol under his pillow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that you could look to Mr. Zigic for protection. Do you mean armed protection, that is, protection with a firearm, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No. Moral support, material, and if I needed protection with weapons, I'm sure he would stand in front of us and protect us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When Mr. Zigic was drunk, would you have trusted him for protection in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He never demonstrated any adverse behaviour towards us, either when he was drunk or when he was sober.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The barbecue that you talked about, or the party that occurred at the end of July, what was the occasion for that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was never a problem for us to have a party, to sit down, have something to eat, drink a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So no special occasion; just friends and neighbours wanted to have a party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Zigic was in the garden, playing, during that party. What was he playing?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: People were playing the guitar, and as I remember, he liked playing the guitar before that, so that was no problem. He took the guitar and had a go on it, played something on the guitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the bandage on his injured finger did not prevent him from playing the guitar at that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, he made the best of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Zoran Zigic cook the food at that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: We all lent a helping hand. We would all take turns barbecuing. Nobody did anything special or just somebody doing something that you could notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zigic take his turn helping with the barbecue?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He was rather tipsy at the time, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that a no, then, or is that a yes? I don't ...

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About how many people came to that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: About ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall the names, please, people who were there?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Myself; my husband, Ivica; his wife, Milka; two young men who played. I don't know, but I think they were both Muslims. I don't know their names. Zoran's daughters, Natasa and Sanja. Nikola would walk around. There was Savka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about Zoran Zigic's kum, Hasan Karabasic? Was he at that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I said there were two Muslims, but I don't know their names. Perhaps I heard their names at the time, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Zigic at that party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Not especially. We were all sitting around and chatting, laughing, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you talk about the Keraterm camp while you were all sitting around?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. That was never a topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you talk about the Omarska camp while you were sitting there around?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Even less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about the Trnopolje camp? Did people talk about the reception centre at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When Mr. Zigic went to sleep around midnight, as you've testified, did you personally see Mr. Zigic asleep in his bed?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Before midnight I didn't see him sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you never -- you did not see Mr. Zigic sleeping in his bed once he left the party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, you saw him sleeping in his bed; or no, you did not see him?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him actually sleeping. I saw him go into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know from your personal knowledge if Mr. Zigic slept through the night?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you think he did. Do you have personal knowledge that he did?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: We were there until between 3.00 and 4.00 a.m. Up until that time, he didn't come out of the house, he didn't leave the house, nor could he have left it, because we would have seen him, because it was just by the front door of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have anything to drink that night?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Fruit juice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did any fights break out at that party, any arguments or altercations?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Zigic would have been seen if he had left the house. Was there only one entrance to that house or was there more than one entrance?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Just one entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there windows to the house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there windows in the front of the house and in the back of the house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there windows on the side of the house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on all three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You testified that the home of Mr. Zigic and his parents was about 700 to 800 metres from the Keraterm camp. How long would it take to drive from that house to the Keraterm camp in a car?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How long would it take to walk from that house to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Half an hour. About half an hour, perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that your son was 15 in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Fourteen, fifteen. I'm not quite sure. He was born in 1978, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: According to your testimony, your son was with Mr. Zigic in an automobile on the 19th of August when Mr. Zigic was shot in the chin. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you knew that Mr. Zigic had a tendency to drink in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it was wartime in Prijedor, right?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Zigic would often carry a pistol; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you allow your son to spend time alone with a man, an armed man, who drinks a lot and who becomes difficult when he drinks, during wartime, and your son was only 14 or 15?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I was at work when Zoran came, took the car. My son was in front of the garage, making a rabbit hut or something like that, and he probably said, "Do you want to come with me?" And whenever it was Zoran, he would always agree to go with him. And Zoran never made any problems. I never had to think about his being drunk or carrying a pistol. On that particular occasion, I wasn't there. I was on the work. Then after work, I went to a funeral. A neighbour's father had died. When I returned home at about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, my son came back home at 6.00 p.m. So I didn't give it any thought about how Zoran was. I knew that he would never do anything to harm my son. He just went off with him and I knew that he would return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that a neighbour's father had died and so you went to a funeral.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When a neighbour had died or someone close to you had passed away in Prijedor, would the funeral be a serious affair or would it be a party?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: A serious affair, and we had to pay our respects to our neighbours. Opposite Zoran's house is where the father of the neighbour had died, and out of respect for our neighbours, we would attend the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At this time, I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Deretic, any additional questions? If you do, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President, I just have two or three questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, when Zoran went into the house to sleep, what condition was he in? The drunkenness, how drunk was he? Was he able to go on his own or did anybody need to assist him? Did someone take him into the house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: He was completely drunk, and my husband helped him, as he would always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In the state he was in, was he capable of jumping out of a window, for example?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Of course not. There was no question of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was Zoran Zigic able to leave the house through the door to pass by you without you noticing him?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't because it's a small village cottage and a small yard. It's not a big place. There's just this one door, and he couldn't possibly leave without us noticing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that that particular evening he played the guitar too.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He always liked to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did he actually play the guitar? Could he play the guitar? Could you describe that to us, this playing of his?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I said that he took up the guitar to play, and I apologise for the expression, but he wanted to have some fun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Until you returned home - you said you returned home at about 3.00 a.m. - did he leave the house at all?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did your husband, Ivica, in that time interval, that is to say, up until he went into the house and your departure, did he enter the house?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether Zoran's parents, either one of Zoran's parents went into the house, or perhaps his wife?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They would go in and out all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In that time frame, did anybody mention anything with respect to Zoran and his sleeping?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Sikic.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have just one inquiry about the paper which was submitted to us. Apparently it has been translated, but it looks like answers to question, as you say, "I am not aware"; "I know." Were you anticipating certain questions and putting the answers for yourself or what?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, if I have come here, you see, I had to know when the war began, when something happened, when Zoran was wounded, when he was with my son, and all this was a long time ago for me to remember without notes to remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you made the scenario for yourself and you were answering the questions?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: No. These are just notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You say, "I'm not aware." Aware of what? This is an answer.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: If I don't know the answer to a question, then it's better for me not to even try to answer it if I don't know the answer. So I thought I'd say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's a good preparation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Sikic, you mentioned that Mr. Zigic had kind of general approval to drive your car because you really trusted him. Did he have a car of his own at that time? At that time, did he have a car of his own? No. Did he have a motorcycle?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think he didn't. I think that he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did he have a motorcycle of his own at that time that you know about?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: A motorcycle? I don't know. I remember seeing a small motorcycle, but I don't remember exactly in what time period, whether it was then or a bit later. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That night that we talked about that you were all in the garden party, just for my enlightenment, what was the last time, if you can place some time on it, that you actually saw Mr. Zigic, that you yourself actually saw him? Just approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I personally saw him just before midnight, between half past 11.00 and 12.00, when he went off to sleep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question is: You said that later on -- I think you said that later on, when the shooting intensified - he had already gone into the house but some of you stayed out until around 3.00, when you went home - that people said, "Oh, it must be mad Ziga shooting up again." Now, why would people say that it must be mad Ziga shooting up again if all those people in the yard, like you, had seen him go in in a very drunken state a couple of hours earlier, and so far as they knew, he was still in bed, still in the kitchen, asleep on the couch? Why would they say, "It must be mad Ziga shooting up again," do you think?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: They were really referring to what other people would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But your interpretation is that they didn't think that themselves; they just thought other people who weren't there might think that? Is that what your answer says?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Ms. Sikic, I too have some questions. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, the question of this note was raised by Judge Riad. We should like to reserve the right to some additional questions. We have the translation but not the original, so we cannot confirm - we may need not more than a minute or two - we cannot confirm whether this really corresponds to what is written in the B/C/S language. We really don't have the original and we don't know what's written in the original notes, and the question has been raised now by His Honour Judge Riad. We have the translation but not the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who has the original, Mr. Stojanovic? I thought it was you. Don't you have the original? The witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think only the Prosecution has the original now. Oh, no, no. Oh, it's been returned to the witness. I see. May I get it? May I look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you could ask the witness for the original and check whether the translation is a good one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecution had it during the break, so we couldn't do it then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a point of clarification, we took the original documents for about three minutes to make copies and then we handed it back either to the usher or to the witness -- to the clerk of the Court, to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We really think there are some minor nuances. One has to do with the question of Judge Riad. Where it says, "I am not aware," the translation in B/C/S is, "I don't know." But this is a minor difference. I don't think it is important. So nothing substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you return the original to the witness, please. So Madam Sikic, the first two notes on your piece of paper should be read as "camouflage uniform" and "red beret"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you take the context -- what prompted you to take those notes? Why did you write down "camouflage uniform" and "red beret"? What was the context?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: I always wanted to say "multicoloured uniform," and then I thought I'd be nervous and I wouldn't remember using the proper term, being "camouflage uniform." And "red beret," I just don't know, because he wore a red beret and everyone didn't wear a red beret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in time and place, where were you going to place this "camouflage uniform" and "red beret"? Do you understand? In space and time, linked to what?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the kind of uniform he wore from the beginning of the war, and I said a red beret because everybody wasn't wearing them. In fact, few people were wearing red berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when you said that he wore this uniform from the beginning of the war, what date would you set as marking the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Power was taken over on the 30th of April, and then a period of one month we were in an atmosphere of expectation and fear, and then when the attack occurred, we knew the war had begun. And then it was all over, as far as I am concerned, regarding dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. You have another note. Let me read it in English, because I have it in English. [In English] "People who participated in the attack of Prijedor and did not respect the Serbian." [Interpretation] Look at the paper now, please. What was the context for this particular note?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: So that I would be able to say who were the people who were taken to camps; those who did not respect the authorities, and people who were attacking Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know the ethnicity of those people, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims. If respect was required of the Serb authorities, then obviously the other party were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another note that you took: "It lasted two or three hours." What was the context? What prompted you to take down that note, to say "two or three hours?" What?

utterances.speaker: SOKA SIKIC
utterances.text: The shooting started after midnight and it went on. Then there was a break and it started again; I don't know how much later. Then it intensified again. And it went on like that for two or three hours. I don't know exactly for how long. I couldn't be that precise, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Madam Sikic. We have no further questions for you. And thank you very much for having come, and we wish you a safe journey home and success in your work. I will ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I thank you. You have been very kind, and I shall be glad if my participation proves useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would ask that a copy of the notes that this witness referred to during her direct testimony be marked as Exhibit 3/242, along with a copy of the draft translation. And when we have a final translation of these notes, we will offer them into admission, Your Honour, as relevant to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We object, Your Honour. We don't think that the suggestion is fair in relation to our code of conduct so far. Endless witnesses have had their own notes and one of the other Defence counsels asked for insight into those notes. They did, and there was no problem about it. These were events that we know took place. So I think this is material that should not be part of the record or part of the evidence. Otherwise, we'll find ourselves in an absurd situation, requesting everybody's notes about all kinds of things to be tendered into evidence. We don't consider this to be a document at all. It is just something jotted down on a piece of paper, just like my notes are here. So we don't think that this can come under what is envisaged by the Rules as documents that could be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any response, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, I do. With all due respect to Mr. Stojanovic, these notes are not just something jotted down on a piece of paper. The Prosecution has compared these notes to the LiveNote transcript, and what we see, beginning on page 64 of the LiveNote transcript, continuing through page 76 of the LiveNote transcript, is that the notes that the witness had in front of her correspond exactly to her testimony, to the order of her -- of the answers that she gave, and so we feel that these notes are relevant then to the credibility of this witness, and we would like to reserve the opportunity to offer them into evidence at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. We have to put an end to this at some point, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber reserves its ruling for the time when we have the final translation. So the document has been marked for identification and once we have the official translation, the Chamber will make a ruling. We also need a little time to think about it. So I think that concludes our work for today. We will resume tomorrow, but it should be said that Judge Fouad Riad will not be with us tomorrow for the first part of the morning, as he has other appointments linked to his health. So we'll be working from 9.20 until 11.00 with two Judges and after that in the presence of Judge Fouad Riad as well. So that's all for today. We'll meet again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
